t: King in Jerusalem, or king of Israel?

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs; Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete agrees)

why: The shorter Hebrew is more likely original; the Greek translator or its Hebrew source probably filled in 'Israel' from 1:12, 'king over Israel in Jerusalem'.

a: who were over Jerusalem before me
p: The Greek and the Qumran copy 4QQoh-b read 'in Jerusalem', as in 2:7 and 2:9.

readings.plain: who were over Jerusalem before me

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs and Codex Vaticanus); 4QQoh-b (4Q110), first century BC, in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription (the letters are visible)
readings.plain: who were in Jerusalem before me

why: 'Over Jerusalem' is the harder reading, since it speaks of rulers before Solomon, of whom there was only David. 'In Jerusalem' is old, since a Qumran copy has it as well as the Greek, but it is the kind of change a copyist makes without meaning to, matching 2:7 and 2:9; no copyist would turn it into 'over Jerusalem'. The difference is small but feeds the debate about who the speaker is (see the note).

t: Madness and folly, or parables and understanding?
p: The Greek has 'parables and understanding' where the Hebrew has 'madness and folly'.

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs and Codex Vaticanus), which also has 'wisdom and knowledge' for 'wisdom'

why: The Hebrew pair returns in 2:12 and 7:25, where Qohelet clearly studies wisdom's opposite. The Greek translator seems to have read the rare word holelot as a form of meshalot, 'proverbs', and the word for folly, spelled here with sin like sekhel 'insight', as 'understanding'.

t: Under the heavens, or under the sun?
p: The Greek has Qohelet's more usual 'under the sun'.
why: Both phrases are Qohelet's (1:13; 3:1 'under the heavens'), with the same meaning. The Greek has made the verse match the commoner phrase; the Hebrew keeps the less usual one.

t: After the king, or after the counsel?
p: The Greek reads 'after the counsel', taking the Hebrew letters for 'king' as an Aramaic word.
why: The royal story (1:12–2:26) makes 'the king' natural. The Greek translator read the same consonants (mlk) in the Aramaic sense 'counsel, advice' (compare Daniel 4:27). The verse is hard in either form (see the note).

a: And I told myself that this too is vapor
t: The Greek adds a saying about the fool's talk
p: The Greek adds one short clause: 'because a fool speaks out of excess'.

readings.en: and I spoke in my heart that this too is vapor
readings.plain: And I told myself that this too is vapor

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs); Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete, puts the added clause after 'this too is vapor'
readings.orig: ἐλάλησα ἐν καρδίᾳ μου διότι ἄφρων ἐκ περισσεύματος λαλεῖ ὅτι καί γε τοῦτο ματαιότης
readings.en: I spoke in my heart, because a fool speaks out of excess, that this too is vanity
readings.plain: And I told myself, because a fool speaks out of excess, that this too is vapor

why: The only Greek plus is the clause 'because a fool speaks out of excess'; the rest of the Greek renders the Hebrew word for word. It has no Hebrew witness and reads like an explanation, probably prompted by the Hebrew yoter, 'more', which the Greek renders 'excessively' (perisson). The Hebrew is shorter and is followed.
b: The Greek also divides the verse differently. It takes the Hebrew 'then more' ('az yoter) with the next verb: 'Why did I become wise? I then spoke excessively in my heart...'. The Hebrew accents join it to 'wise', as the Plain English Translation does: 'Why then have I been so very wise?'

t: Apart from me, or apart from him?
p: The Hebrew says 'apart from me'; the Greek reads 'apart from him', meaning God.

readings.en: outside of me / more than I

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs and Codex Vaticanus); the Syriac, as reported by Seow and others

why: The two readings differ by one letter (mimmenni, mimmennu). 'Apart from him' fits 2:24 and 2:26 well, and many modern translations follow it, but that is exactly why a copyist or translator might have made the change; 'apart from me' is the harder reading and fits the king's claim to have tried everything (2:10). Both are possible. In the same verse Rahlfs' Greek reads 'who will spare' for 'who will enjoy', and Codex Vaticanus 'who will drink'.
b: Chuts mimmenni is 'outside of me', or, in later Hebrew, 'more than I'. On that reading the king says: who has eaten and enjoyed more than I have? So he can speak with authority about pleasure (KJV: 'more than I'). With 'apart from him', no one can eat or enjoy apart from God, which fits 2:24 and 2:26.

a: Who knows whether the spirit of human beings goes up above, and whether the spirit of animals goes down below to the earth?
t: Whether it goes up, or which goes up?
p: The Hebrew letters can be read 'whether it goes up' or 'which goes up'; the Masoretic vowels choose the second. Both are questions.

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs and Codex Vaticanus, εἰ, 'whether'); Jerome's Latin (si, 'whether'); followed by most modern translations
readings.en: whether it goes up... whether it goes down
readings.plain: Who knows whether the spirit of human beings goes up above, and whether the spirit of animals goes down below to the earth?

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), vowels הָעֹלָה and הַיֹּרֶדֶת; followed by the KJV
readings.orig: הָעֹלָה הִיא לְמָעְלָה... הַיֹּרֶדֶת הִיא לְמַטָּה
readings.en: which goes up above... which goes down below
readings.plain: Who knows the spirit of human beings, which goes up above, and the spirit of animals, which goes down below to the earth?

why: The consonants are the same in both readings; only the vowels under the first letter differ (the article 'the one which' or the question word 'whether'). 'Whether' fits the 'who knows' and the flow of 3:18–20, and the oldest translations read it that way. With 'which', the verse is still a question, but it seems to take for granted that the human spirit rises. Many scholars think the Masoretic vowels were chosen to avoid seeming to doubt that. The Plain English Translation follows the Greek and Latin vowels but keeps every Hebrew letter.
b: This is a case where the Plain English Translation departs from the Leningrad Codex's vowels, not from its letters. The vowel signs were added between about AD 600 and 1000; they record a careful reading tradition but not the original writer's pronunciation. See the note on this verse and the traditions card on the chapter page.

a: his eye never has its fill
p: The written text has 'his eyes'; the reading the Masoretes marked (Qere), the verb and the Greek have 'his eye'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, read form (Qere), Leningrad Codex; Greek (Rahlfs)
readings.plain: his eye never has its fill
his eyes never have their fill

why: The verb tisba' is singular, so the reading tradition's 'his eye' fits the grammar; the meaning is the same. The singular also matches 1:8, 'No eye has its fill of seeing'.
